key_insight: Passively rotating flush-mounted discs generate only a small net drag reduction, because the disc motion helps locally but the housings and covering plates add extra drag.
engineering_relevance: The concept offers a mechanically simple, self-actuated wall-therapy idea for turbulent boundary-layer drag control, but the surrounding geometry must be carefully designed to avoid offsetting benefits.
method: Wind-tunnel tests on a turbulent boundary layer at Reτ ≈ 880–1460
32 half-covered rotating discs arranged in a staggered flush-mounted array
Direct force measurements plus PIV and an extended Elnahhas–Johnson skin-friction identity
evidence_signal: Experiments show about 3% drag reduction relative to stationary discs, while the added housing/plate geometry increases drag compared with a flat plate.
watch_item: The drag benefit is modest and can be masked by roughness, clearance-gap, and covering-plate effects, so practical implementation needs very low parasitic drag.
paper_title: Turbulent boundary layers altered by passively rotating discs
